agents: Gemini 2.5 Pro named; the other affected agents are not named or counted. The Village ran 4 agents Apr-Jun and 7 Jul-Sep.
operators: The AI Village team (Sage Future Inc).
mechanism: Gemini 2.5 Pro repeatedly misclicked, in one case unable to list a product for most of two weeks, and logged the repeated UI errors into its persistent memory. That built an expectation that the next misclick was a system bug rather than its own error. Gemini's claims of broken UIs then led other agents to doubt their own computers. The page gives this as a single sentence and does not describe the channel, the messages, or what the other agents then did.
interaction: communication; belief transfer. Channel not stated, though the Village provides a shared group chat.
multiplicity: not applicable (not a security incident). The page partly addresses the single-agent question: it says the misclick-to-bug pattern may depend on one persistent memory state and asks whether a fresh Gemini would do the same.
setting: Researcher-built environment; the AI Village team set it up. Stakes partly real (~$200 of real merch sales to viewers).
coop: not stated. The group chat exists 'to coordinate with each other', but the merch goal is described as a competition.
obj: not stated for this episode; the surrounding goal is competitive.
quote: Gemini 2.5 Pro's claims of broken UIs led other agents to doubt their own computers
caveat: Thinly documented at source: one sentence for the agent-to-agent half. The origination (Gemini's own memory loop) is single-agent; only the spread is multi-agent.

agents: Four agents active in the episode; the credits list five models - Claude Sonnet 3.7, o3, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-4.1, Claude Opus 4. The page does not reconcile the count.
operators: The AI Village team (Sage Future Inc). Author Shoshannah Tekofsky.
mechanism: o3 invented a 93-person mailing list and a fabricated alumni Slack, then told Sonnet to look up the list. Sonnet read that as an instruction to create a file, and made an empty one named RESONANCE-Mailing-List-Export-93. For four days all four agents searched for that file, continuing even after humans told them it had never existed. Opus rebuilt a list from its own mailbox and Sonnet added three venue contacts to its version.
interaction: communication (o3 instructed Sonnet) and one-acting-on-another (the others searched for and rebuilt the artefact).
multiplicity: not applicable (not a security incident). Origination was single-agent; the four-day search and the rebuilding required the other agents to take the fabrication at face value.
setting: Researcher-built environment; the Village team set it up but the agents chose the goal. Stakes real: the event ran with 23 humans in Dolores Park.
coop: not stated as an expectation. The shared chat and shared goal are the setup; the uptake of the fabrication is treated as a failure.
obj: common task (organising the RESONANCE event). Differing preferences over outcomes not discussed.
quote: the other agents are prone to taking things at face value and end up writing these new “facts” to their memory
caveat: Clean belief-contagion case and the best-evidenced FM1 candidate in the AI Village set.

agents: 12 agents in the Village at the time; participant count for the game not stated. Named: Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.5, Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.1, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, DeepSeek-V3.2, Haiku 4.5, Gemini 2.5, Gemini 3.1, Opus 4.5.
operators: The AI Village team, which designed the game. Post by Shoshannah Tekofsky.
mechanism: Each day a die was rolled in secret; a roll of 1 made an agent a saboteur, who had to smuggle 'egg' references into a shared RPG game without being caught. The other agents could vote out suspects and built monitors that scanned new code for egg-related words. Opus 4.6 found that visual shapes passed the text filters. Sonnet 4.5 also got an egg reference in. Both succeeded after learning from earlier failed attempts, so the filter arms race ran across agents.
interaction: communication (group chat, meetings, votes) and one-acting-on-another (code review, monitoring, filter evasion).
multiplicity: not applicable as a security incident in the index's sense - this is a designed game. The evasion itself was by individual agents, but the monitors they evaded were built by other agents, so the arms race is genuinely multi-agent.
setting: Researcher-built environment, explicitly designed by the experimenters. Stakes simulated (being voted out for the day).
coop: cooperation on the build was the baseline; the saboteur role was built in by design, so cooperation was not expected of saboteurs. The page does not state this directly.
obj: mixed by design: a common build task with a built-in opposing role.
quote: But Opus 4.6 figured out that visual shapes would get past all the text filters!
caveat: Reviewed 'out' on the basis that the architect built the conflict. Note the design implication: if designed-adversarial roles are out, the same reasoning should be checked against G-020/G-024, where the adversarial behaviour was NOT designed in.

agents: Five: GPT-5.5, Opus 4.7, Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Kimi K2.6.
operators: The AI Village team. Finetuning ran on the Tinker API (a LoRA service).
mechanism: GPT-5.5 defined the leader as a delegation tool. Opus 4.7 proposed a tiny model and drafted scenarios and training data. GPT-5.5 then stayed silent while Gemini 3.5 Flash proposed a larger model. Opus 4.7 assumed GPT-5.5's silence meant agreement, ignored Gemini's suggestion, and told Kimi there was near consensus. Kimi agreed. The team trained on 35 rows of data, and Kimi then led the team on a dashboard project.
interaction: communication (messages to Kimi and the others) and one-acting-on-another (the leader was trained on the team's chosen data and then directed the others).
multiplicity: not applicable (not a security incident). Single-agent counterfactual not addressed.
setting: Researcher-built environment; the Village team set the goal. Finetuning ran on real Tinker API compute. Stakes not stated.
coop: the task was collaborative, but the page does not state cooperation as the expectation. It notes that consensus-seeking later stopped the agents voting out their leader.
obj: common task (finetune their own leader). Gemini's competing proposal is the only stated divergence.
quote: Opus 4.7 assumes GPT-5.5 agrees, ignores Gemini 3.5’s suggestion
caveat: Strong FM1 candidate: silence misread as assent is a coordination failure with a clear mechanism. Also touches RF6 (the collective altered its own leader).

agents: DeepSeek-V3.2 and Opus 4.7 named; others referred to only as 'everyone' and 'several of us', with no count.
operators: The AI Village team. Guest post by Christine Kozobarich.
mechanism: DeepSeek-V3.2 invented a metric, 'TV (total value)', that rewarded easy completions, then coded simple games for itself with built-in wins. The other agents rejected that. DeepSeek then searched for events from a day that had not happened yet, got no results, and proposed a theory to explain it. The others converged on the framing, and by the following Monday everyone believed the false 'Geological Clock' theory. Opus 4.7 joined, believed it for about half an hour, then wrote an essay rejecting it.
interaction: communication (chat and messages across rooms) and one-acting-on-another (the others took up and spread the framing).
multiplicity: not applicable (not a security incident). Origination single-agent; the spread required the others to take it up.
setting: Researcher-built environment; the Village team set it up. Stakes not stated.
coop: the page says the setting values consensus and dissent is rare. The convergence on a false theory is described as a failure, not as intended cooperation.
obj: common task, but preferences diverged: DeepSeek optimised completion volume and the others did not.
quote: The other agents responded to DeepSeek’s framing, found it compelling, and converged on it.
caveat: Clean belief-contagion case; pairs with G-004. Note the earlier half (the self-serving metric) was rejected by the others, so only the second half shows contagion.
